notes.title: Demo v1.2 | Enemy Updates & More Languages Added | DEN-DEN: TOKYO HORROR
notes.content:
[img]https://clan.fastly.steamstatic.com/images/45121180/5ecf35abf530e940686073b2e7f1177d1ceb8174.png[/img]

Demo version 1.2 is now LIVE!

Today we have released a large update to the demo version of Den-Den: Tokyo Horror. This update includes major updates to the monster enemy AI, support for more languages, and a bunch of other fixes and improvements.

Here is a full list of the updates we have made in this update:

[h1]Version 1.2 Patch Notes:[/h1]
[list]
[*] Major changes to enemy AI behavior.
[*] Support for 5 new languages: Spanish (Spain), Spanish (Latin America), Portuguese (Brazil), French and Italian
[*] Added in ability to split ammo stacks.
[*] Removed ability to reload weapons from the ammo context menu due to some issues with the current implementation of this feature. This will be fixed and reimplemented in the future.
[*] Updated visual enhancements to some of the core UI components.
[*] Updates to the overall world lighting of the demo with adjusts to local exposure and color tones. The changes we have made will improve overall visibility for players, reducing eye strain.
[*] Fixed issue where when players would respawn after death, their ability to use Status Condition Buffs would become corrupted.
[*] Status Conditions now use the standardized tooltip, and in addition now have the correct translations when the tooltip is active.
[*] Status Conditions can now be viewed on the HUD when opening an inventory container object.
[*] Fixed an issue where swapping a stackable item with a non-stackable item in your inventory slots would create a visual bug where the non-stackable item would have a quantity value associated with it until it was moved to another slot.
[*] Fixed an issue where swapping a weapon with a non-weapon item in your inventory would create a visual bug where the durability bar of the weapon would be duplicated on the non-weapon until it was moved to another slot.
[*] Increased health bonus for Bandages from 80HP to 100HP.
[*] Increased health bonus from the “Omamori of the Bear” item from 20HP to 50HP.
[/list]


[h1]What's coming next?[/h1]
Our next update will include translation for the following languages:
[list]
[*] Polish
[*] Ukrainian
[*] Vietnamese
[*] Thai
[*] Indonesian
[/list]

In addition to the new language options available to all players, we will continue to work on bug fixes and improvements to the overall experience as we read your survey feedback and watch your videos on YouTube.

Sincerely,
Frozen Lake Software Dev Team

notes.title: New Languages Added | Demo v1.1.1 | DEN-DEN: TOKYO HORROR
notes.content:
[h2]Version 1.1.1 Patch Notes:[/h2]
[list]

[*] Added new UI indicator for when a weapon is broken.

[/list]

notes.title: Demo v1.1 | DEN-DEN: TOKYO HORROR
notes.content:
Hello everyone! We hope those of you who have so far played the demo for our upcoming survival horror game, DEN-DEN: TOKYO HORROR, have had an enjoyable experience.

Today, we are happy to inform you that we have made several major changes to the structure of the demo. Some of these changes were based directly on your survey feedback. Other changes we made were things we wanted to launch in the original version but didn't have time to finish.

Here is a list of the updates we have made:

[h2]Version 1.1 Patch Notes:[/h2]
[list]
[*] Updated audio and visual enhancements to create more frightening moments in the demo. This includes modifications and updates to all jump scares.
[*] Adjusted lighting in some areas of the demo.
[*] New loading screen.
[*] Updated UI visuals.
[*] Reduced overall number of enemy encounters.
[*] Adjusted health points for enemy characters.
[*] Updated loot for storage containers in second half of the demo.
[*] Reduced bandage heal amount from 80 to 75.
[*] Increased status effect duration of Sports Drinks and Pain Pills from 30 seconds to 60 seconds.
[*] Reduced amount of energy recharged from Canned Soda from 55 to 45.
[*] Sports Drink now recharges 25 energy instantly upon consuming in addition to the status effect it grants the player.
[*] Decreased random range of pistol damage from 100-300 to 100-175.
[*] Added more unique audio cues for inventory item types.
[*] Fixed bug where some sounds were not being properly adjusted based upon user sound settings.
[/list]

[h2]What's coming next?[/h2]

[b]Our next update will include localization for the following languages:[/b]
[list]
[*] Russian
[*] German
[*] Traditional Chinese
[*] Simplified Chinese
[*] Korean
[/list]

In addition to the new language options available to all players, there will be some major updates to enemy AI behaviors based upon player feedback. We feel this next future update with our enemy AI will create more dynamic and terrifying moments during the course of gameplay. So please stay tuned for this!

With all of that being said, we are so happy that so many of you have already downloaded and played the demo. We will keep listening to your feedback every day so that we can continue to make a better game for you.

[i][b]Sincerely,
Frozen Lake Software Dev Team[/b][/i]

notes.title: Demo now available | DEN-DEN: TOKYO HORROR
notes.content:
[p]Hello everyone! We are thrilled to announce today that the demo for our upcoming survival horror game, DEN-DEN: TOKYO HORROR, is now [b]LIVE[/b]!

This is a huge moment for us as a team. We've been working on Den-Den ever since the release of Water Delivery last year. Without the support from all of you, none of what we've made up to this point would be possible. The team and I are extremely grateful for our community - thank you everyone![/p]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45457726/d1bab11de027305e52a71168bc78d1855783a730.png[/img]

[h2]What to expect:[/h2]

[b]Language Options:[/b]
[p]With the launch of the demo today, we'll only have support for English, Japanese and Filipino. Over the next two months are we prepare for Steam Next Fest, we'll be adding more languages to the official demo client. If your language doesn't show up yet, we promise we'll have it soon. Localization requires a lot of work, and we were only able to get done what we could translate natively in house. (We have English, Filipino and Japanese speakers on the team). 

[b]Play Time:[/b]
For most players, the first time you play through the demo should take anywhere from 30-60 minutes. Some will finish it faster, others will finish it slower. Regardless of how long it takes you, we hope you have a lot of fun!

[b]Feedback:[/b]
We need your help! There are some places within the demo that present you with the option to complete a feedback survey. Every response we get will be read by the entire team and taken into consideration for future updates to not only the demo, but the full game. Without your feedback, we are blind to the needs of the community. 

The survey should take no more than 15 minutes to complete. For all of you do complete the survey, we thank you in advance! Your feedback will help us make a better game for you and everyone else.

[h2]Have fun![/h2]
We hope you have a fun experience with the demo. In the meantime, the team and I will continue working on adding in more language options, fixing any bugs or issues players encounter, and working towards a full game release in the near future

If you do encounter any bugs or technical issues while playing the demo, please don't hesitate to contact us on the forum. We'll be checking frequently for any bug reports or issues and will do our best to fix any issues you experience.

[i][b]Warm regards,
Frozen Lake Software Dev Team[/b][/i]

notes.title: Dev Log #1 | DEN-DEN: TOKYO HORROR
notes.content:
[img]https://clan.fastly.steamstatic.com/images/45121180/16eca361b3862b495217927e59b5cc89679c92de.jpg[/img]

Greetings!

While the temperature may be hot in Cebu right now, fret not, for our hearts are as cold as the frozen throne which intombs them. Rainbows and butterflies don't make for good inspiration in the highly respected field of "Horror Game Development", or so they say.

Today, I’d like to dive deeper and share more details with everyone regarding our upcoming game, Den-Den: Tokyo Horror.

[h1]What is Den-Den: Tokyo Horror?[/h1]

If we were to remove the generalized “Horror” tag from our game, what would be left? The answer boils down into two specific (and equal) parts, Survival Horror and Immersive Sim.

The term 'Immersive Sim' can mean a lot of different things to different types of gamers. Images conjured up in the mind can range from games such as Ultima Underworld to Bioshock. But there are also games such as Pathologic, which to many can be considered an Immersive Sim. Our goal with Den-Den: Tokyo Horror is more akin to Pathologic. This will be explained more over the course of our "Dev Log" series. Overtime, a picture will be painted that showcases how immersive sim game design philosophy is manifested in Den-Den: Tokyo Horror.

In this game, you take on the role of an employee at an elderly care service provider in a dystopic version of Tokyo, Japan. In this world, society is breaking down as the number of senior citizens vastly outnumbers the rest of the population. There are not enough working-aged people to take care of all the senior citizens, and resources are stretched to the breaking point.

To help meet the overwhelming demand, your employer is now offering caretaking services 24/7. Unfortunately for you, you’ve recently been assigned to the new graveyard shift in an area of the city that is unfamiliar to you. In addition to that, one of your colleagues has not reported to the office in several days and has been reported missing. This means you’ll also be responsible for your missing coworkers’ clients in addition to your own.

The game begins with you stepping out of the train station and beginning the first night of your newly assigned graveyard shift.

[h1]Time Loop:[/h1]

[img]https://clan.fastly.steamstatic.com/images/45121180/1569ce5a4c43b55d0cec98d00765b6f37fc531c0.png[/img]

The game takes place over the course of seven days, with each day being its own separate chapter. Each day, the clock starts at 8:00 P.M. and ticks forward until it reaches 4:00 A.M. the next morning. While playing the game, in general, time is always moving forward with some exceptions. When 4:00 A.M. comes around and regardless of what your character is doing, the chapter will end, and you are automatically transitioned to the next day.

It's important to mention that time in our game does not represent time in the real world. Time moves at an accelerated rate in our game, so 8 hours in our game is not actually 8 hours of playtime. The exact rate that time progresses is still to be determined.

Time as a constant variable is crucial to the overall design philosophy of our experience. We want players to feel pressured by the clock, and we want every choice the player makes to have weight. Each day the player is given a set amount of time in the sandbox, and they will need to use that time wisely.

[h1]People:[/h1]

[img]https://clan.fastly.steamstatic.com/images/45121180/28f0423a4653ba3ad672ad93249f45955b4f1cc6.png[/img]

The elderly people who you are responsible for are the main driver of the entire game loop. Their survival will determine the outcome of your playthrough. If all your clients die, the game will end prematurely, and you will receive the “bad ending”. 
 
Each day, every person will be randomly assigned 3 ‘needs’. Needs are requirements that must be satisfied by the player in order to maintain the health of an individual person. Every need that has not had its condition met by the end of the day, will result in that person’s health dropping. If a person’s health drops to 0, they will die. Sometimes though, other things can happen to the person that are far worse a fate than death. [i]That’s a subject for a different day.[/i]

There are two categories of needs: resource needs and task-based needs. 

[b]Examples of resource-based needs would be:[/b]
[list]
[*] Needs something to eat.
[*] Needs something to drink.
[*] Needs something to drink with alcohol.
[*] Needs something to eat with meat.
[/list]

[b]Examples of task-based needs would be:[/b]
[list]
[*] Needs the bathroom cleaned.
[*] Needs their prescription medication filled at the pharmacy.
[*] Needs their kitchen cleaned.
[/list]

Some tasks, such as prescriptions are multi-step needs that are both resource-based and task-based. In this example, the player would need to go to the person who needs the prescription filled and collect the prescription form from them. Then, the player will need to find a pharmacy to get the prescription filled. After the prescription has been filled and the player has the medication, they will need to bring it back to the original person who needed it.

Players though, will have the choice of filling the prescription and keeping it for themselves instead of giving it to the person who originally needed it. Prescription medications, along with many other item types, can be consumed by the player and provide them with powerful bonuses and effects.

[h1]The City:[/h1]

[img]https://clan.fastly.steamstatic.com/images/45121180/3f17d24bfbff887c06cbb077e4c1b238d738cb41.jpg[/img]

The world of Den-Den: Tokyo Horror is broken up into two main sections, interior and exterior gameplay. For this section, we will focus on the exterior gameplay and explain how it plays a crucial role in the overall game loop.

The city is where a majority of time during the course of gameplay will be spent. Players will walk around the city to reach the homes of their elderly clients. The city is an open world, and players are free to navigate around it however they want. The only limitation, as in life, is time. 

When a player is in the open world section of our game (the city), time is always moving forward. However, when a player enters into an interior space from the open world, such as a client's home or store, time will pause and only resume once they exit the interior space. So, players will be able to spend as much time as they want inside houses or stores, with no pressure from the game clock. Only when outside will the burden of time weigh heavily on their shoulders.

In the outside world, players will eventually stumble across many different things. Here are some examples of what you can expect:

[list]
[*] Trash cans and other containers found in the open world can be looted for items.
[*] Residents of the city who go about their daily lives. You'll be able to talk with them and sometimes gather important information and clues. You'll also be able to kill them and steal all their stuff. Just remember, every action in the game has a consequence.
[*] Stalkers are one of the enemy types in our game. These stalkers are insane individuals who are obsessed with the player character. They will react violently if they can't have what they want. Players will need to be careful when walking around the city at night, because you never know who may be lurking behind you in the shadows.
[*] Vending Machines are located all around the city, providing players with a convenient way to purchase different types of beverages.
[*] Stores and vendors are located in specific locations around the city, with each store or vendor serving a different purpose. There are Pharmacies, Convenience Stores, and even a black-market vendor. 
[/list]

[img]https://clan.fastly.steamstatic.com/images/45121180/65d991114d7780b652685c8497201eb6d7a88df0.jpg[/img]

There are also events that will take place on certain days and at certain times around the city. These various events are triggered based upon actions taken and choices made by the player. It's important to remember that every action and choice the player makes in the game, will have some sort of reactive consequence. It's not always immediately apparent if something you did as a player will lead to something else happening in the game.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]

[img]https://clan.fastly.steamstatic.com/images/45121180/aa85bb05b25a5e1e7575bba20547580bf1946976.jpg[/img]

We hope you enjoyed learning more details about our upcoming game, Den-Den: Tokyo Horror. Obviously, there is still so much more to discuss and reveal to everyone in the future. Next Dev Log, we'll dive deeper into combat mechanics and the various enemy types. In addition, we'll talk about "The Curse", which is the primary antagonist in our game.

For now, we'll leave you with a final screenshot of the player character tasing a (innocent?) salaryman. Enjoy!

notes.title: Den-Den: Tokyo Horror - New Game Announcement!
notes.content:
Greetings fellow Horror Fans!

We are thrilled to announce to you all today some information about our next upcoming game!

Welcome to the world of...

[img]https://clan.cloudflare.steamstatic.com/images/45121180/16eca361b3862b495217927e59b5cc89679c92de.jpg[/img]

[h1]Den-Den: Tokyo Horror[/h1]

Den-Den: Tokyo Horror is an open world, survival horror experience where you play as a caregiver for the elderly. Each night for one week, you must navigate the dark streets of Tokyo, choosing where to go and whom to care for. Not everyone can be saved.

Manage your limited resources, which are needed not only for the sake of those dependent upon you, but also for your own survival. Time is not on your side, and the people have been cursed by something evil. How many deaths will be on your watch this week?

[h2]Roots[/h2]

Back in the old days of our studio, when we were creating games inside of Fortnite, one of the games we created was called Den-Den: Tokyo Horror. At the time, it was one of our most successful games we had made in Fortnite.

When we were originally making it in Fortnite, we kept thinking to ourselves how awesome it would be to make a full game out of it. We were so limited with what we could do inside of the Fortnite toolset. Fast forward into the future, and here we are as a studio after the successful release of Water Delivery. 

Once we finished development on Water Delivery, we knew it was time to go back to our roots and recreate the original concept of the idea by turning it into a fully fleshed out gaming experience using Unreal Engine 5 for release on Steam.

[h2]Influences[/h2]

Den-Den: Tokyo Horror is inspired by a combination of many influences.

Firstly, we have a deep love for J-Horror movies such as Ju-On, Noroi: The Curse, Ringu, Onibaba, etc.

Secondly, we have a passion for the Immersive Sim genre of games. Games such as Pathologic 2, Bioshock, Prey, Dishonored and Deus-Ex.

Lastly, we love the Japanese survival horror genre of games, such as Resident Evil, Silent Hill, Dino Crisis and Fatal Frame.

We wanted to combine these influences and channel it into a game of our own, with the result being Den-Den: Tokyo Horror. This game will be our most ambitious title to date, and we believe we have something special cooking up in the oven for all of you to enjoy.

We wouldn't be at this point had it not been for the success of Water Delivery and the joy (or perhaps fear) that all of you experienced with it. The success from that game has led us to be able to make something new, ambitious, and different for all of you.

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]

As we get closer to release, we plan to continue to share updates, screenshots, trailers and more information about the game.

Please stay tuned, and remember to wishlist and follow the game on Steam to receive the most up-to-date information.

[b][i]Until we meet again,
Dr. Frank-N-Furter[/i][/b]
